prompt_free_text:
This paper tackles an important and underexplored problem: helping users manage privacy risks in voluntary online self-disclosure. The work combines three components that are individually useful and collectively quite compelling: a new span-level taxonomy and annotated corpus of self-disclosures, a token/span identification model, and a new generation task of “self-disclosure abstraction” motivated by a user study. The paper is ambitious in scope and clearly grounded in a real user need rather than only benchmark performance. I found the overall direction timely and potentially impactful, especially because most prior work either focuses on narrow PII detection or on sentence/post-level disclosure classification rather than actionable span-level assistance.

The strongest aspect of the paper is the framing of privacy support as something more nuanced than redaction. The distinction between aggressive anonymization and utility-preserving abstraction is well motivated, and the examples make the intended use case intuitive. The inclusion of an HCI study is also a real strength: it surfaces the mismatch between annotator-defined “risk” and user-perceived sensitivity, and this insight directly motivates the abstraction task. That iterative, human-centered loop is valuable and differentiates the paper from purely technical privacy-detection work.

The dataset contribution also appears meaningful. A taxonomy of 19 categories spanning both attributes and experiences is broader than much prior work, and the decision to annotate contextualized spans rather than minimal entities is sensible for downstream assistance. The corpus size is moderate but respectable for a careful in-house annotation effort. The chronological split is also a good design choice for reducing temporal leakage and approximating deployment. The identification results are promising, especially token-level F1 above 75 for the multiclass setting and above 81 for binary on sentence-segmented inputs. The per-class breakdown is informative and shows where the task is easier versus still quite difficult.

That said, I have several concerns about the technical rigor and the strength of some claims.

First, the identification setup is somewhat underspecified and the evaluation leaves important questions unanswered. The paper reports token-, partial-span-, and exact-span F1, but it is not always clear whether these are micro- or macro-averaged, especially in the multiclass setting. Table 2 says multiclass results are averaged over classes excluding O, but Table 3 suggests per-class scores only for 17 classes, while the taxonomy has 19 categories. Name and Contact seem omitted because they are handled separately with LUKE/Presidio plus a sentence classifier, but then the headline claim of a 19-category identification system is somewhat misleading unless the hybrid pipeline is evaluated end-to-end across all 19 categories. As written, the main sequence tagger seems to cover only 17 categories, and the paper does not provide a unified end-to-end evaluation including the external detectors. This matters because the rare but high-risk categories are exactly those where practical systems need reliability.

Second, the annotation methodology raises some concerns about selection bias and coverage. Only posts that both initial annotators agreed contained personal disclosure were retained for span annotation. This likely improves annotation efficiency, but it may bias the corpus toward clearer, more explicit disclosures and remove borderline or ambiguous cases that are crucial in realistic deployment. Since the system is intended to assist users on naturally occurring posts, the exclusion of disagreement cases may inflate performance and reduce ecological validity. Relatedly, the paper does not report inter-annotator agreement for either the initial filtering stage or the span/category annotations. Given the conceptual ambiguity of self-disclosure and the user-study finding that users often disagree with annotators about what is risky, agreement statistics are essential.

Third, the user study is interesting but should be interpreted more cautiously. The sample size is small (21 participants), and the reported “82% positive outlook” is encouraging but not especially robust. More importantly, the study appears to use manually annotated images of model outputs rather than a live system, which is fine for formative work but should temper claims of real-world applicability. The participants were also asked to provide posts that had raised privacy concerns or that they were hesitant to publish, which may enrich the study but also selects for users already sensitized to privacy. I would encourage the authors to frame this as an exploratory formative study rather than strong validation of deployment readiness.

Fourth, the abstraction task is novel and potentially valuable, but the current experimental setup has substantial validity issues. The training and evaluation data for abstraction are generated by LLMs, with ChatGPT used for train/eval references and GPT-4 for test references. The best-performing model is then described as being “distilled on GPT-4 generated abstractions.” This creates a somewhat circular benchmark: the task definition, supervision, and references are all induced by proprietary LLMs rather than humans. Human evaluation partially mitigates this, but only partially. It remains unclear whether the model is learning a genuinely useful privacy-preserving rewriting behavior or simply imitating the stylistic preferences of the teacher models. This concern is amplified by the very small abstraction dataset: 159 training posts, 25 eval, 50 test. The number of span instances may be larger, but the paper should report it explicitly. As it stands, the abstraction results feel preliminary.

Fifth, the automatic metrics for abstraction are not very convincing for this task. BLEU and ROUGE are weak proxies for privacy reduction and utility preservation, and the paper itself acknowledges diversity and semantic fit as central desiderata. The human evaluation is therefore the key evidence, but it is limited: one author conducts the evaluation on 60 sampled instances, which introduces a serious risk of bias. At minimum, multiple independent raters should be used, with agreement reported. Also, the privacy score of 3.19/5 is described as moderate reduction, which seems fair, but the paper’s broader framing sometimes sounds stronger than the evidence supports. If the system only moderately reduces privacy risk, that should be emphasized clearly, especially because overtrust in such a tool could itself be harmful.

Sixth, the paper’s ethical discussion is thoughtful in some respects but too optimistic in others. The claim that model failures “do not pose additional risks” because they tend toward overprotection is not fully convincing. False negatives clearly pose risk by failing to flag sensitive disclosures. False positives may also have harms: they can normalize surveillance-like scrutiny, frustrate users, or disproportionately burden communities where disclosure is necessary for support-seeking. The user study itself found oversensitivity and subreddit-specific norms to be important. Similarly, the statement that no harms would disproportionately impact marginalized populations seems too strong given that marginalized users often rely on contextual self-disclosure for support and may be especially affected by misclassification or over-abstraction. I would like to see a more nuanced discussion of these risks.

There are also several methodological details missing or unclear. The paper should report the number of annotated spans in train/val/test, not only overall. It should clarify whether comments are annotated jointly with posts and how context boundaries are handled. It should provide hyperparameters for fine-tuning, decoding settings for generation, and whether results are averaged over multiple random seeds. For the identification model, comparisons against stronger baselines would help: for example, a CRF-based tagger, a DeBERTa encoder, or prompting-based LLM baselines. For abstraction, a direct GPT-4 prompting baseline seems especially important, since the task supervision itself comes from GPT models and the practical question is whether a smaller local model can approach teacher quality. Without such a baseline, it is hard to assess the value of the fine-tuned Llama system.

I also think the taxonomy itself deserves more critical examination. Some categories appear overlapping or socially contingent, such as Relationship Status versus Husband/BF and Wife/GF, or Health versus Mental Health. The rationale for splitting some categories and merging others is not fully justified. The user study suggests that sensitivity is contextual and personalized, yet the taxonomy is fixed and universal. That is acceptable for a first dataset, but the paper should acknowledge more explicitly that category boundaries are normative design choices rather than objective truths.

Despite these concerns, I think the paper has substantial merit. The problem is important, the span-level dataset is useful, the user-centered motivation is strong, and the abstraction task is genuinely novel. My main reservation is that the paper currently combines a solid identification contribution with a much more preliminary abstraction contribution, and the latter is not yet evaluated rigorously enough to support strong conclusions. If accepted, I would want the authors to tighten claims, clarify the end-to-end system boundaries, and better document annotation quality and evaluation methodology.

The most important improvements would be: report inter-annotator agreement and more annotation statistics; evaluate the full 19-category hybrid identification pipeline end-to-end; add stronger baselines and seed variance; clarify the abstraction dataset size in span instances; include human-written abstraction references or at least multi-rater human evaluation by non-authors; compare against direct prompting baselines; and substantially deepen the discussion of failure modes, personalization, and subgroup harms. An error analysis would also be very valuable, especially for low-performing categories like sexual orientation and relationship status, and for cases where users disagreed with the model.

Overall, I view this as a promising and original paper with clear practical motivation and several strong ideas, but with notable weaknesses in evaluation rigor and claim calibration. My assessment is positive on the identification/data side and more cautious on the abstraction side. If the conference values novel, interdisciplinary work and is comfortable with some components being exploratory, this paper could be a worthwhile acceptance. If the bar is primarily technical rigor and mature evaluation, the current version may fall short.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper studies privacy protection for online self-disclosures on Reddit via two tasks: (1) span-level identification of self-disclosure and (2) abstraction of detected disclosures into less specific alternatives. It introduces a 19-category taxonomy and a corpus of 2.4K Reddit posts with 4.8K annotated disclosure spans. For identification, the authors fine-tune RoBERTa-large and report best token-level F1 above 75% (81.78% in binary, 75.30% in multi-class on sentence-segmented inputs), though exact span F1 is much lower. They also conduct a small formative user study with 21 Reddit users, reporting generally positive perceptions. Motivated by this study, they define a new generation task, self-disclosure abstraction, and fine-tune Llama-2 7B with several prompting/training variants using LLM-generated references. Human evaluation suggests the best abstraction model yields moderate privacy reduction, high utility preservation, and high diversity.
strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: user-side privacy protection for voluntary self-disclosure rather than only PII redaction or attribute inference.
Introduces a reasonably broad taxonomy of 19 self-disclosure categories and a span-level annotated corpus, which is a useful resource directionally.
Moves beyond pure benchmark evaluation by including a user study that surfaces practical concerns such as oversensitivity, personalization, and subreddit context.
The identification task is clearly formulated, and the paper reports multiple evaluation granularities (token, partial span, exact span), which is more informative than a single metric.
The abstraction task is novel and practically motivated; generating multiple candidate abstractions is a sensible design choice for user-facing systems.
The paper is generally well motivated and connects NLP modeling with HCI/privacy considerations.
weaknesses: The empirical evidence for real privacy protection is weak: the paper mainly measures lexical overlap and subjective ratings rather than actual reduction in re-identification or attribute inference risk.

The abstraction dataset and evaluation rely heavily on LLM-generated references (ChatGPT/GPT-4), making the task definition and success criteria partially circular and potentially biased toward mimicking teacher model style.
The abstraction training/evaluation data are very small (159/25/50 posts), which limits confidence in generalization and makes the generation results preliminary.

Identification performance is overstated in the narrative: token F1 is decent, but exact span F1 is only around 49 multi-class / 54 binary, with very poor performance on some sensitive classes such as sexual orientation.

The user study is small, qualitative, and not integrated with a deployable automatic pipeline because outputs were manually annotated into images for participants; this weakens claims of real-world applicability.
Important annotation details are missing or insufficiently quantified, especially inter-annotator agreement for both post selection and span/category labeling.
The taxonomy mixes heterogeneous concepts (e.g., relationship status vs husband/BF vs wife/GF; health vs mental health), raising concerns about label consistency and downstream ambiguity.

No meaningful comparison is made against stronger baselines for span detection (e.g., CRF heads, instruction-tuned sequence labeling LLMs, or simpler regex/PII baselines on overlapping categories) or for abstraction (e.g., direct prompting of GPT-4/ChatGPT at test time).

The paper does not adequately analyze harms from false negatives, which are critical in privacy settings; the ethics statement's claim that failures mainly tend toward overprotection is not supported by the reported results.
methodological_flaws: Selection bias in corpus construction: only posts that both initial annotators agreed contained disclosure were retained for span annotation. This excludes borderline/negative cases and may distort the training/test distribution, inflate apparent performance, and reduce ecological validity for deployment where many posts are ambiguous or non-disclosing.

Lack of reported inter-annotator agreement is a serious methodological omission. Without agreement statistics for post-level filtering, span boundaries, and category labels, it is impossible to assess annotation reliability for a subjective task.

The claim that model failures 'do not pose additional risks' and mainly 'tend towards overprotection' is scientifically unsupported and contradicted by nontrivial false-negative rates implied by span F1 around 50 and weak per-class results on sensitive categories. Missing a disclosure can clearly pose additional privacy risk in a user-facing warning system.

The abstraction evaluation does not validate privacy reduction against an operational threat model. Human Likert judgments of 'privacy reduction' are not equivalent to reduced identifiability, reduced attribute inference, or reduced linkage risk.

Using ChatGPT for train/dev references and GPT-4 for test references introduces teacher/model mismatch and possible evaluation contamination of the task definition. The system is effectively trained to imitate one LLM family and judged partly against another, rather than against human-authored gold abstractions.

Automatic metrics for abstraction (BLEU/ROUGE) are poorly aligned with the stated objective of privacy-utility tradeoff. Higher lexical overlap may even conflict with stronger abstraction, so these metrics provide limited empirical validity.

Human evaluation for abstraction appears to be conducted by one author on 60 sampled instances, which raises substantial risk of evaluator bias and low reliability; no inter-rater agreement or blinded multi-annotator protocol is reported.

The sentence-level segmentation result may partly benefit from simplifying the task distribution rather than genuinely improving contextual understanding; the paper does not analyze whether sentence splitting harms cross-sentence disclosures or context-dependent cases.

The hybrid identification pipeline for rare classes (LUKE/Presidio/regex plus a sentence classifier) is not evaluated in a unified end-to-end manner across all classes, making it hard to assess actual system performance.
The paper makes broad applicability claims, but all data come from Reddit, English, and mostly U.S.-centric annotation/user study settings; external validity is therefore limited.
